newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Yr/Yr Italy CPI rises, petrol costs worry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Yr/Yr Italy CPI rises, petrol costs worry.

text.p: Italy's headline inflation figure rose for the first time in a year in July but the increase was largely due to statistical reasons with price pressure remaining subdued, national statistics office Istat said on Tuesday.

However there is increasing concern in government circles that recent dollar strength could damage Italy's inflation restraint, with petrol companies pumping their lira prices higher in response to exchange rate weakness.

Istat said the annual consumer price index rose 1.6 percent last month from 1.4 percent in June. At a month-on-month level, inflation was unchanged. The figures confirmed preliminary data from 11 Italian cities released in late July.

Istat said the rise in the annual rate was explained by good CPI data in July 1996, when prices fell 0.2 percent from June to 3.6 percent year-on-year. This meant that even though the July 1997 monthly rate was stable, the annual rate was forced higher.

Across the basket of goods used to work out the inflation figure, prices remained little-changed last month, with food costs and entertainment costs both dipping 0.2 percent over June while housing and utility charges rose 0.3 percent.
Istat said average annual inflation in July, calculated over the last 12 months, stood at 2.4 percent, below the government's official CPI target for 1997 of 2.5 percent.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi predicted earlier this year that inflation would be between 2.1-2.2 percent in 1997 from 3.9 percent in 1996.
But there is growing unease over the rampant dollar, which has risen more than 20 percent since the start of the year to 12-year highs against the lira.

Istat said on Tuesday it did not think the 'super-dollar', as it has been dubbed by the Italian media, would have a huge impact on inflation, despite the fact that almost all raw materials are priced in dollars.

"It's clear that costs will go up, but Italian firms have shown they can work over the medium term and can therefore draw up price plans, absorbing oscillating costs," said Enrico Giovannini, head of Istat's economic department.
However, the government is particularly worried by petrol charges, with Italy heavily dependent on oil imports.
Oil firms have been swift to jack up pump prices in response to dollar gains, hiking the price of four-star petrol to a record high 1,935 lire ($1.05) per litre.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government on Tuesday condemned the increase and demanded an urgent meeting with the country's oil industry body.

"The government believes these rises are unjustified," the government said in a statement following a cabinet meeting. "(It) believes that the trend and current excessive level of prices are without parallel in the European Union," it added.
Oil firms have defended their actions, saying they have passed on only part of the added costs to their customers.

Franco Bernabe, managing director of Italian energy giant Eni, told La Repubblica newspaper on Tuesday that he saw little risk for inflation, predicting that the price of crude oil would soon fall, compensating for the strong dollar.
"I'm convinced that (Italian) inflation is falling in a structural manner," he said. $1 = 1,839 lire
